parts.title: Reporting a Lost Bag
parts.context: A woman phones a railway company's lost property office to report a bag she left on a train the previous evening.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a railway company's lost property office about a bag she left on a train. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 1 to 5.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Westmere Railways lost property office, Gareth speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Oh, hello. Um, I think I left a bag on one of your trains, and I'm really hoping someone's handed it in.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Right, well, you've come to the right place. I'll take a few details first, and then I'll have a look at what's come in. Can I start with your name?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Yes, it's Helen Prothero.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: And could you spell the surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: P… R… O… T… H… E… R… O.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: P… R… O… T… H… E… R… O… E?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: No, there's no E at the end. Everyone adds one. It just finishes with the O.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Sorry about that. I've taken it off. And a contact number?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: My mobile's best. It's oh-seven-seven-one-two… six-four-eight, three-oh-nine.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Oh-seven-seven-one-two, six-four-eight, three-oh-nine. Lovely. Now, when did you travel?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: It was Wednesday evening… so that would be the seventh.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: The seventh. So that's two days ago?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Oh, no, hang on, I'm muddling it up. Wednesday was when I travelled up for the conference. I came back yesterday, on Thursday, so it was the eighth. Sorry, it's been a long week.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Not a problem. Thursday the eighth. And do you know which train it was?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: It was from Redbourne to Kingsford. I was booked on the six-fifteen, but the last session overran and I missed it by about a minute, so I ended up getting the next one, the six forty-five.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: The eighteen forty-five from Redbourne. That's the slow one, isn't it? Stops at every station.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: It certainly felt like it.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: And was it a direct train, or did you have to change anywhere along the way? Sometimes bags end up being handed in at a different station.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: No, it was direct, thank goodness. I don't think I could have coped with a change. I just sat there with my eyes closed until Kingsford, and then, well… I got off without it.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Do you remember which part of the train you were in? It helps the cleaning teams know where to look.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Well, after the week I'd had, I'd have loved to be in first class, but I wasn't. The standard carriages were absolutely packed, so I went and found a seat in the quiet coach, right at the front.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: The quiet coach, that's useful. They're usually less cluttered, so things get spotted. And where did you put the bag? Under the seat?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: No, it's too bulky, it wouldn't fit under the seat. I put it up on the luggage rack, right above my head. That's exactly why I forgot it. I couldn't see it.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: That's the most common one, honestly. Out of sight, out of mind.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 6 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Right, now I need a description of the bag itself. What sort of bag is it? A suitcase, a rucksack…?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: It's a holdall. My son calls it my gym bag, but it isn't really, I've never taken it near a gym. It's a proper holdall, with two handles and a long shoulder strap.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: A holdall. And what colour is it?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Well, it looks black in some lights, and the man at the station desk last night wrote down black, but it definitely isn't. It's navy blue, with a cream strap.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Navy blue, cream strap. Is there anything that makes it stand out? A name tag, a label?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: There used to be a name tag, but it tore off ages ago and I never replaced it. But there's a little metal key ring on the zip. It's shaped like a lighthouse. My husband says it looks more like a rocket, but it's a lighthouse. We bought it on holiday in Cornwall.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: A lighthouse. That's actually really helpful. It's those little details that let us match an item to the right person.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: And what was inside it? Anything valuable?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Well, luckily my laptop wasn't in it, I'd put that in my backpack, and my purse was in my coat pocket. But my camera was in there, and that's what I'm really upset about. All the photos from the week are on it. The rest is just clothes and a paperback.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: I'll mark the camera as the main item of value. Let me just check the system for yesterday evening… Nothing matching yet, I'm afraid, but please don't worry. Anything found on the late trains is collected at the end of the line, and it usually reaches us here a day or two later.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Oh, that's good to know. And if it does turn up, how do I get it back?

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: You can either come and collect it from this office, at Kingsford station, or we can post it to you. There is a fee, I'm afraid, either way.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: How much are we talking about?

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: To collect it in person, it's twelve pounds. It used to be ten, but it went up in April. If you'd rather we posted it, it's the twelve plus postage, and for a bag that size you'd be looking at another fifteen or so on top.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: In that case I'll definitely come and pick it up myself. I only live twenty minutes away. Twelve pounds it is.

transcript.speaker: Gareth
transcript.text: Just bring some photo ID with you, a driving licence or a passport, and we're open eight till six, Monday to Saturday. And I'll ring your mobile the moment anything comes in.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Thank you so much, Gareth. You've been really kind.

parts.title: The Mill Lane Allotment Scheme
parts.context: A council officer speaks to residents at a public meeting about a new community allotment scheme on a former plant nursery site.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a council officer talking to local residents about a new community allotment scheme. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 14.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 11 to 14.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming out on such a wet night. My name's Joanna Pike, and I'm the community projects officer at Ashworth District Council. I'm here to tell you about our new allotment scheme at Mill Lane, which opens to plot holders in March.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: For those of you who don't know it, the site used to be a commercial plant nursery. It closed about six years ago, and it's been empty ever since. Well, empty apart from a lot of brambles.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Now, quite a few of you have asked why we went for Mill Lane rather than the field behind the leisure centre, so let me deal with that first. I know some people were hoping the new site would be easy to get to by bus, and I have to be honest, it isn't ideal from that point of view. The nearest stop is a good fifteen minutes' walk away.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: There's also a rumour going round that the land was given to the council free of charge. That's not quite right, I'm afraid. We lease it from the Haddon Estate, although, admittedly, the rent is very modest.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: What actually decided it was, first of all, the ground itself. When we had samples analysed, the soil came back as being of exceptionally high quality, which I suppose is the result of decades of the nursery digging in compost. And the second thing, which saved us a great deal of money, is that because it was a nursery, there's already a mains water connection on site. So we haven't had to pay to bring a supply in from the road.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: One thing Mill Lane is not, though, is sheltered. The northern edge is very exposed, and the winds there can be fierce, so we'll be planting a native hedge along that side over the winter.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Right, the money. A full plot will cost sixty pounds a year, and a half plot thirty-five. So what do you get for that? Well, people often assume that water is included. It isn't, I'm afraid. Each row of plots has its own meter, and the cost is divided between the plot holders in that row, so it's charged separately.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: What the fee does cover is unlimited use of everything in the communal tool store: spades, forks, wheelbarrows, even a rotavator. And every autumn, the council will drop off a load of well-rotted manure at every plot, which, if you've ever tried to buy the stuff, you'll know is well worth having.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: In our pilot scheme at Brook Street, we also gave out free packets of seeds to new tenants, but sadly the budget won't stretch to that this time round. And there's a gardeners' association, which I'd really urge you to join. But that's run by the volunteers themselves and it has its own small subscription, so it isn't part of what you pay us.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Now, you should all have a copy of the site plan, so let me take you round the different areas, because each one has its own arrangements.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Starting at the main gate on Mill Lane itself. You don't need to book a time to visit; you can come whenever you like between dawn and dusk. At Brook Street, people got into the habit of leaving the gate open during the day while they were working, and we had several thefts. So at Mill Lane, it has to be kept locked at all times, even when you're on site. You'll each be given the code.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Just inside the gate is the orchard: twelve apple and plum trees that the nursery left behind. We did consider allocating the trees to individual plot holders, but we decided against it. When the fruit's ripe, anyone who has a plot is welcome to help themselves. Within reason, please. The volunteers prune the trees on Saturday mornings, but that doesn't mean you can only go in at weekends; it's open every day.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: In the middle of the site there's a wildlife pond. You might expect us to have banned strimmers and mowers around it, to protect the frogs and newts, but in fact our ecologist says occasional cutting is perfectly fine. What we do insist on is that young children never go near the water on their own. If you bring your kids, an adult must be with them there at all times.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Next to the car park, you'll see eight raised beds, built at waist height. These aren't for general use. They're set aside for gardeners who use a wheelchair, or who find kneeling and bending difficult. There's a set of long-handled tools stored right beside them, too, so nobody has to carry heavy equipment across the site.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Beyond those is the polytunnel, which is for raising seedlings in spring. It's unlocked all week, but space on the benches is limited, so you can't just turn up with your trays. You'll need to reserve a bench in advance through the online system.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And finally, at the far end, by the back gate, are the compost bays. A volunteer has to be there to check what goes in, otherwise we end up with plastic and goodness knows what else, so they're only open on Saturdays and Sundays.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And while we're down at that end: some of you will remember the bonfires at Brook Street. Please be aware that they're not permitted anywhere at Mill Lane, and that includes the compost area. The houses are just too close.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Application forms are on the table by the door. There's an open day on the first Saturday in February if you'd like to look round before you sign up. Right, I think I've talked for long enough. Are there any questions?

parts.title: A Sleep and Memory Experiment
parts.context: Two psychology students review the procedure and results of an experiment they ran on the effect of sleep on memory, and plan their report and presentation.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Maya and Josh, discussing an experiment they carried out on sleep and memory. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 24.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 21 to 24.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Right, Maya, shall we go through the procedure section first? Dr Hollis said it has to be clear enough for someone else to repeat the study exactly.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Sure. So, recruitment. We were originally going to put posters up all over campus, remember?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: And we got precisely three volunteers out of that.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Right. And the emails to the first-year class lists didn't do much better. It was really the item in the department's newsletter that got us most of our people. Something like thirty of the forty came through that.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Yeah, and I think we should be upfront about it, because it might affect who took part. People who actually read the newsletter are probably more motivated than average.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Good point. Okay, then the learning session. Everyone studied the same sixty pairs of unrelated words. Where do we say that happened? Because it changed, didn't it?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: It did. We'd booked the lab, but then the postgrads needed it for their own testing. And you suggested letting people learn the words in their own rooms…

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Which would've been a disaster. No control over noise or anything. So in the end we used that quiet room in the library, the one on the second floor.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Yes. Okay. And then the sleep group went home to bed, and we measured their sleep. I still wish we'd been able to borrow the EEG headset from the sleep lab.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Josh, we weren't trained to use it, and it would've cost a fortune. The wristband was fine. Everyone in the sleep group wore one overnight, and it gave us total sleep time.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: And the sleep diaries?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: We asked them to fill one in, sure, but half of them didn't bother, so they really weren't our main measure. I'd mention them in a footnote at most.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Fair enough. Then, twelve hours after learning, everyone came back. And before the actual memory test, we did the alertness check.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Which ended up being just the questionnaire. We'd planned a reaction-time task as well, but it took fifteen minutes per person and we didn't have the time. So it was the questionnaire on its own, rating how awake they felt. And then the recall test.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 25 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 25 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Okay, results. So the sleep group did better, as we predicted. But honestly, what I didn't see coming was how big the gap was.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Really? The studies we read found roughly a twenty percent advantage for sleep, and ours was eighteen. That's pretty standard. No, what got me was where the advantage came from. Nearly all of it was on the pairs that people had rated as the hardest to learn. On the easy ones, the two groups were almost level.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Hmm. Yeah, when you put it like that, the overall difference is in line with the literature. It's the hard-pair thing that's odd. And the wake group did about as badly as we expected, so there's nothing strange there.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Speaking of the wake group, I was worried that some of them might have had a nap during the day, which would mess everything up.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: I don't think napping was the problem. We asked every one of them, and nobody said they'd slept. And they were all tested within ten minutes of the right time, so the timing's fine too. What does bother me is the two who said they'd gone over the words in their heads on the bus.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Oh, yeah. They were actually practising them on purpose. That's a real issue. We should have told everyone not to do that.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Definitely. We'll mention it.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: In the limitations section, or as some kind of confession?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Limitations. Hollis appreciates honesty, as long as it's in the right place.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Now, limitations. I think the obvious criticism Hollis will make is the sample size. Forty people isn't many.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Everyone says that, but forty's not unusual for this kind of study. What worries me far more is that the sleep group learned the words in the evening and the wake group learned them in the morning. So time of day is mixed up with sleep. We can't separate the two.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: And they were all undergraduates, aged eighteen to twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: That's a limitation, sure, but it's not specific to us. Most memory research uses students. It's the timing that's our own fault.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Okay, but I don't think the timing thing makes the whole study worthless. Far from it. And we couldn't have tested everybody in the evening; the whole design needs a night's sleep for one group and a day awake for the other. But look, the questionnaire showed both groups felt equally alert when they were tested. We can use that to argue the time of day probably didn't make much difference.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: That's true. It doesn't solve it completely, but it helps. Okay. What about participant seventeen? Fifty-nine out of sixty. My instinct is just to take them out.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Josh! We can't just delete data because it's inconvenient. Hollis would go through the roof.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Well, could we email them and ask whether they'd seen the list before?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: We promised everyone anonymity. We don't even have their names linked to the numbers.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Fair point. So we leave them in and flag it up when we discuss the results.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Exactly. And then the presentation. I thought we'd spend most of it on the wristbands, since no other group measured sleep that way.

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Hmm, it's only ten minutes, though, and the method's the least exciting part. I'd rather build it around the hard-pair result. That's what people will actually remember.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Yeah, okay, you've convinced me. And ideas for future studies?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Just one slide, right at the end. Nothing more.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Great. So I'll draft the procedure tonight, you take the results, and we swap on Thursday and check each other's sections?

transcript.speaker: Josh
transcript.text: Deal. And we can put all the wristband details in an appendix, so that work still gets some credit.

parts.title: Bioluminescence in Deep-Sea Animals
parts.context: A marine biology lecturer explains how deep-sea animals produce light, the different functions this light serves, and some applications of the research.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about bioluminescence in deep-sea animals. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. Today we're heading down into the deep ocean, below about two hundred metres, where sunlight barely reaches, to look at bioluminescence: the production of light by living organisms. It's not a rare curiosity, by the way. Down there, it's thought that roughly three-quarters of all animals can make their own light.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, how is it done? In most cases the light comes from a chemical reaction. A light-emitting compound, known generally as a luciferin, reacts with oxygen, and that reaction is speeded up by an enzyme called luciferase. In some jellyfish, the reaction is set off by calcium, and students often write that calcium is what the luciferin combines with. It isn't. Calcium is only the trigger.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What's remarkable is how efficient this is. An old-fashioned light bulb loses most of its energy as heat. Bioluminescence loses almost none that way, which is why it's often described as cold light. For an animal that may go weeks between meals, that efficiency really matters.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Then there's colour. In shallow coastal waters, you'll find quite a lot of green light, and a handful of species produce yellow. But in the deep ocean, the light is overwhelmingly blue, and that's because blue wavelengths travel the furthest through seawater. Most deep-sea animals, in fact, can't even see other colours.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And how do animals switch the light on and off? Well, that varies. Many species control it directly through their nervous system, so a flash can last a fraction of a second. Others, which have glowing tissue that's permanently lit, cover it with folds of skin, rather like shutters, or rotate the light organ inwards. Either way, the light is under the animal's control, and that's important for everything I'm going to describe.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: I should add that not every glowing animal makes its own chemicals. Some appear to get their luciferin from their diet, from the food they eat. And others, the anglerfish being the classic example, don't produce the light themselves at all. Instead, they house bacteria inside specialised organs, and it's those that glow. The fish supplies nutrients; the bacteria supply light. A neat arrangement.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Right. So that's the how. Now for the more interesting question: why? Why would an animal spend energy, however little, on making light, when doing so might also reveal it to something hungry? Biologists generally group the functions into three: hiding, defending and hunting. Plus one more I'll come to at the end.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's start with hiding. In the upper part of the deep sea, there's still a faint glow coming from the surface. Now, to a predator looking up from below, it isn't an animal's colour, or even its size, that gives it away. It's its silhouette, that dark outline against the dim light above. So many fish and squid have light organs along their bellies, and they adjust the brightness to match the light from above. The outline simply disappears. This is called counter-illumination.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Defence next. In shallow water, a squid that's under attack squirts out ink. But think about it: in complete darkness, a cloud of black ink is pretty useless. So some deep-sea squid, and certain shrimps too, release a glowing mucus instead. The predator is left lunging at a bright, sticky cloud while its prey slips away into the dark.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And then there's a rather clever strategy that's been nicknamed the burglar alarm. Some jellyfish, when they're grabbed, produce a spinning display of flashing light. You'd assume the aim is to frighten the attacker. Well, it's not so much about scaring it off as attracting attention. The flashes can be seen a long way off, and they bring in a larger predator, which may well go after whatever's attacking the jellyfish.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, hunting. The anglerfish I mentioned dangles its glowing lure in front of its mouth, and curious prey swim straight towards it. But my favourite example is the dragonfish. Remember I said most deep-sea animals only see blue? Well, the dragonfish has organs under its eyes that give out red light. Its prey can't detect it, so the dragonfish is effectively using a private searchlight.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And the fourth function: communication. Lanternfish have rows of light organs called photophores, and the pattern differs from one species to another. For a long time, people assumed these patterns mainly helped the fish to stay together in shoals. More recent work, though, suggests that their real purpose is to help individuals recognise potential mates of their own species in the dark.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: I should say that studying all this is extremely difficult. Many of these animals are fragile, and when they're hauled up in nets from several kilometres down, they rarely survive the journey, and their light organs are often damaged. What's more, the moment you shine a torch at them to take a photograph, you swamp their own light completely. So a lot of what we now know comes from cameras on remotely operated vehicles, which can sit quietly in the dark for hours and record extremely faint flashes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, a word on why this research matters outside marine biology. The genes for luciferase have been put to use well beyond the sea. One early application was in tests to detect bacteria in food, and that still goes on. But by far their most important use today is in medical research, especially on cancer. Scientists insert the gene into cancer cells, so that they can watch, in a living animal, how tumours grow and spread. So, from the bottom of the ocean to the hospital, which is quite a journey.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Right, next week, we'll look at sound in the deep sea. Please read chapter seven before then.
